web_evidence.note: The authorized publisher excerpt sustains third-person narration across separate scenes centered on Cutter, Ramun, Chavez, and weapons technicians, repeatedly reporting characters' thoughts without a participating narrator.

web_evidence.title: Tom Clancy Writing Styles in Clear and Present Danger
web_evidence.note: The book-level point-of-view analysis explicitly describes changing scene focalization as generally third person attached to each character, with third-person omniscient biographical sketches.

search_log: Searched "Clear and Present Danger" Tom Clancy excerpt and first chapter; found and opened the Penguin Random House title page and its library-marketing publisher excerpt.

Searched "Clear and Present Danger" with third person, narrator, point of view, omniscient, and alternating-narration terms; opened BookRags' whole-book POV discussion and found no credible claim of first-, second-, or alternating-person base narration.
Searched Google Books and Archive.org for previews; a Google Books listing surfaced but its page returned HTTP 403 when opened, and no usable Archive.org text was found.
Reviewed an informal WordPress review that called the novel third-person, but omitted it from evidence because the publisher excerpt and dedicated POV analysis were stronger.
person_note: The diagnostic quotes repeatedly move among Ryan, Chavez, the President, and other characters in external third-person narration, often with access to their thoughts. First- and second-person forms occur only in dialogue, maxims, or generic idioms. The authorized opening excerpt independently shows the same multi-character third-person method, and the whole-book POV source explicitly confirms that the scene changes remain third person. No evidence indicated sustained first- or second-person base sections; the only limitation is that the Tier A prose source covers the opening rather than the entire novel.
